The Jurassic Period. From two hundred and one to one hundred and forty-five million years ago, this was the golden age of dinosaurs, when sauropods reached colossal sizes—creatures like Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus—and theropods grew into fearsome predators such as Allosaurus. Pangaea rifted into northern and southern continents, and oceans flooded vast inland seas. The period is named after the Jura Mountains in the Alps.

Sauropods dominated terrestrial ecosystems as quadrupedal herbivores with long necks and whip-like tails, some exceeding thirty metres in length. Theropod predators like Allosaurus and Spinosaurus hunted the sauropods, and some theropods evolved feathers and eventually took flight as birds. Pangaea rifted apart, opening the Atlantic Ocean and creating separate northern and southern continents, which altered climate and biodiversity across the globe.

Conifer forests remained the dominant vegetation, though flowering plants—angiosperms—appeared late in the Jurassic but remained rare. Ammonites, spiral-shelled cephalopods, and other marine life flourished in the shallow inland seas that covered much of the continents. Pterosaurs, flying reptiles distinct from birds, soared overhead, with some species having wingspans exceeding ten metres.

The Jurassic follows the Triassic Period, when dinosaurs first emerged, and precedes the Cretaceous Period, the final age of dinosaurs, with dinosaurs themselves representing the iconic vertebrates that dominated this era.
